topic_and_scope: This document analyzes electro-elastic instabilities (EEI) and electro-elastic turbulence (EET) in electrokinetic flows of viscoelastic fluids, highlighting experimental and numerical work, gaps, and potential applications in microfluidics, heat transfer, and environmental remediation. It also outlines concrete avenues for future research to advance fundamental understanding and practical implementation of EEI/EET phenomena under electrokinetic driving.
main_themes: Fundamental mechanisms and characterization of EEI/EET in electrokinetic (EK) flows, including onset thresholds, role of Weissenberg/ Deborah numbers, geometry, and velocity profiles.

Methodological and modeling advances to study EEI/EET, addressing HWNP, stabilization methods, fixed-point data analysis, and multiscale (micro–macro) simulations for viscoelastic fluids under EK forcing.

Translation to practice: potential applications and optimization of EEI/EET for enhanced mixing, microscale heat transfer, and electrokinetic remediation, including considerations of real-world rheology and geometric constraints.
main_findings: There is experimental and numerical evidence of electro-elastic instability (EEI) and electro-elastic turbulence (EET) in electrokinetic flows of viscoelastic fluids, with onset and behavior influenced by parameters such as Wi, EDL thickness, flow geometry, and local shear/extension conditions.

Mixing enhancement under EEI/EET is not universally observed; studies report conflicting results—some show improved mixing or transport, while others show negligible or reduced mixing—indicating a strong dependence on geometry, rheology (shear-thinning, yield stress), and how EK flow interacts with elastic stresses.

key_gaps.description: Limited fixed-point, time-resolved experimental analyses of EEI/EET under electro-osmotic driving; reliance on interface observations without comprehensive μ-PIV-based flow-field statistics to quantify instability onset and turbulent-like states.

Absence of validated micro–macro multiscale simulations that resolve polymer microstructure evolution under electrokinetic driving (overcoming HWNP) and couple with EK-driven flow fields to reveal onset mechanisms and transport implications.

future_directions.title: Establish fixed-point, time-resolved flow-field characterization of EEI/EET in electro-osmotic microchannels using μ-PIV
future_directions.rationale: The field needs rigorous statistical analyses of fixed-point fluctuations and global flow-field evolution to define EI/EET thresholds and dynamics under EK driving. Implement standardized μ-PIV experiments in cross-slot, T-junction, and expansion/contraction geometries across a range of Wi, EDL thicknesses, and viscoelastic fluids. quantify velocity fluctuations, spectra, correlation functions, and mixing metrics to connect flow states with transport outcomes.

future_directions.title: Develop and apply multiscale micro–macro simulations for viscoelastic fluids under electrokinetic forcing
future_directions.rationale: Current studies rely on continuum models that neglect microscopic polymer evolution. Build coupled micro–macro frameworks (e.g., FENE-P/Oldroyd-B with polymer conformation dynamics) integrated with electro-osmotic body forces and EK boundary conditions. Address HWNP with advanced stabilization (beyond log-conformation), and validate against fixed-point flow measurements to reveal molecular pathways driving EI/EET and their impact on mixing and transport.

future_directions.title: Perform comparative studies between electrokinetically driven EI/EET and pressure-driven EI/EET
future_directions.rationale: Understand how plug-like EK velocity profiles alter instability onset, turbulence characteristics, and mixing efficacy relative to parabolic, pressure-driven flows. Map thresholds in terms of Wi, De, and Re across geometries, and assess consequences for heat and mass transfer efficiency. This will clarify whether EK driving inherently limits or enhances chaotic transport compared to traditional driving methods.

future_directions.title: Systematic rheology-informed exploration of non-Boger fluids under EEI/EET in EK systems
future_directions.rationale: Real-world fluids exhibit shear-thinning, yield stress, and thixotropy, which may modulate EI/EET differently from Boger fluids. Systematically test representative biofluids and polymer/surfactant solutions to identify rheological regimes that promote or suppress EEI/EET. Develop practical guidelines for selecting fluids and operating conditions to optimize mixing or transport in microfluidic devices.

future_directions.title: Investigate EEI/EET effects in porous media and electrokinetic remediation contexts
future_directions.rationale: Extend EEI/EET insights to electro-osmotic flows in soils and sediments to evaluate potential improvements in contaminant mobilization and removal efficiency. Design experiments in soil analogs or transparent porous media, quantify dispersion and uptake under varying electric fields, and determine whether chaotic EK-driven flows can enhance remediation performance in low-permeability substrates.

future_directions.title: Develop flow-control strategies to harness EEI/EET for tunable microfluidic mixing and reactions
future_directions.rationale: Leverage real-time flow data and possibly ML-based control to toggle between stable and chaotic regimes, achieving desired mixing rates or suppressing unwanted fluctuations. Implement feedback schemes using voltage modulation, electrode geometry adjustments, or surface charge patterning, validated with μ-PIV and mixing metrics in representative microfluidic platforms.

future_directions.title: Geometric optimization and surface-charge patterning to tailor EI/EET onset and transport
future_directions.rationale: Elastic instabilities arise from the interaction of elastic stresses with streamline curvature; curved geometries and zeta-potential patterns strongly influence EI/EET. Systematically explore channel shapes, curvature distributions, and patterned surfaces to identify designs that maximize or minimize mixing/heat transfer as required, while ensuring manufacturability at the microscale.
